data.body: Registration survives the wake as a deadline-only reservation; claim, wait and next refuse a younger or unqueued claimant with reserved-for; dead, lapsed, self and disjoint waiters never block; brief names who waits.
data.title: Waiter reservation: older live waiter keeps a freed file for a bounded window

data.claim: Reuse the wait registry; a woken waiter keeps a deadline-only reservation since its wait process exits before it claims. Early glob release before merge is unsafe so holder side is advice only.
data.question: FIFO queue for glob-refused claims

evidence.note: research R1f866a8b96 (THEORETICAL design; the probe is the regression suite). Against unfixed main tests/test_claim_fairness.py: 9 failed, 5 passed (A/B/C: C's claim after the release succeeds instead of 'reserved for B').
ddflow brief --item B-fix-claim-fairness read; no decision binds the wait/claim registry; D-shared-globs/D-readme-current respected (README updated, knob count 139->140).
commit a42135f: lifecycle/waits fairness + tests/test_claim_fairness.py (14 tests); full suite 3622 passed on the worktree (config knob pending t6 lease)

chunk_findings.detail: `_join_line`'s docstring promises "Never fails the refusal," and the companion `_leave_line` guards the queue-write path with `try/except (OSError, ValueError, TypeError)` — evidence that the `WT` (waits) state operations can raise exactly those errors. `_join_line` has no such guard: it calls `WT.queue(...)` bare. `_refuse_if_reserved` calls `_join_line` *before* returning the `O.refused(...)`, so any failure in `WT.queue` propagates out of `_join_line` → `_refuse_if_reserved` → `_early_refusal` into the claim path. Concrete scenario: the waits/line state file (or its directory) is unwritable (read-only repo, full disk, concurrent lock) and `WT.queue` raises `OSError`; instead of the caller receiving the intended `item.claimed` / `reserved-for` refusal (and the "your place in line is kept" message), the claim raises an unhandled `OSError`. The refusal is lost and no reservation is recorded — the opposite of the documented contract. Wrapping the `WT.queue` call in the same `try/except` used by `_leave_line` restores the "advisory, never fails the refusal" behavior.
chunk_findings.title: `ddflow/api/lifecycle.py` `_join_line`

chunk_findings.detail:
`queue` is documented as advisory ("an unwritable registry means no queue, never a failed claim"), and the guard only wraps `mkdir` and the `.gitignore` write:

```
    try:
        path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        ignore = path.parent.parent / ".gitignore"
        if not ignore.exists():
            ignore.write_text("*\n", "utf-8")
    except OSError:
        return
    _write(w)
```

`_write(w)` — the actual registration write — is outside the `except OSError`. If the registry directory already exists (so `mkdir` succeeds) and `.gitignore` already exists (so no write is attempted), any error from `_write` (read-only directory, ENOSPC, EACCES on the JSON file) propagates out of `queue` and turns the refused-claim path into a raised `OSError`, exactly the failure the docstring promises cannot happen. Concretely: a repo where `.ddflow/.../.gitignore` was created on an earlier run and the directory is now mounted read-only causes a refused `claim` to raise instead of simply proceeding without a queue place. Either wrap `_write` in the same `try/except OSError`, or move it inside the `try` block.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/waits.py:queue() (`_write(w)` at the end of `queue`)

chunk_findings.detail: The path is built by concatenating then sanitizing `f"{agent}-q-{item}"`, which is not injective, so distinct `(agent, item)` pairs can map to the same file. Example: `queue(repo, "a", "b-q-c", ...)` and `queue(repo, "a-q-b", "c", ...)` both produce `<dir>/a-q-b-q-c.json` (the sanitizer keeps `-`). The same collision occurs for names that differ only in characters the sanitizer maps to `_` (e.g. agent `"a/b"` vs agent `"a_b"` with the same item). Consequences: `drop_queue(repo, "a-q-b", "c")` (called from `take_place`) unlinks the place held by `("a","b-q-c")`, and `queue`'s `since`-inheritance reads that unrelated file, attributing another agent's original join time to this one. An unambiguous encoding (e.g. length-prefix or hash of `agent` and `item`) avoids the aliasing.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/waits.py:_queue_path()

chunk_findings.detail: The added conjunct `isinstance(w.woken, bool)` makes the record validator depend on a field that is not present in waiters written before this change and that may not be a Python `bool` in the persistence format. Given a previously-registered waiter such as `{"pid": 42, "until": 1234.5}` (no `woken` key), evaluating the predicate either raises `KeyError`/`AttributeError` on `w.woken`, or the whole conjunction evaluates false, so the waiter is classified as not live. Consequently the reserved-for check no longer sees the older waiter, and a younger claimant is allowed to claim the freed file — exactly the scenario the reservation feature is supposed to prevent. The same falsification occurs if `woken` is persisted as the integer `0`/`1` (a common SQLite/row/msgpack representation), because `isinstance(1, bool)` is `False`: a woken waiter (`1`) is silently dropped and its reservation is lost. The check should tolerate absent/non-boolean stored values (or the writer/migration should guarantee the field), otherwise pre-existing or non-JSON-persisted waiters lose their reservation.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/waits.py:261

chunk_findings.detail: The test's stated purpose is that the reservation survives when the waiting process is *gone* ("deadline-only reservation", per the module docstring). But `_wait_until_woken` runs `A.wait` inside a `threading.Thread` of the pytest process, so the `Waiter` registration carries the (still-alive) pid of the test process. When the thread returns, only the thread ends; the pid stays alive for the rest of the test, and `WT.live_waiters(proj)` therefore reports the waiter as live for the ordinary liveness reason, not because woken waiters are gated by deadline only. Concretely: if the implementation regressed back to dropping a woken waiter whose pid is dead (i.e. it kept pid-based liveness after wake), every assertion here (`kept == [(B, "TB", True)]`, `TC` refused `reserved for B`, `TB` claimable by `B`) would still pass, so the headline behavior "registration survives the wake even after the process exits" is not actually exercised by any test in the file (`test_a_dead_waiter_never_blocks` covers dead-but-never-woken only). To test the real feature the wait would have to run in a subprocess that exits after being woken.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_claim_fairness.py::test_a_woken_wait_keeps_its_place_after_its_process_is_gone

chunk_findings.detail: `_join_line`'s own docstring promises "Never fails the refusal", and it sits directly on the refusal path (`_refuse_if_reserved` calls it *before* constructing/returning the `O.refused(...)` Outcome), yet unlike `_leave_line` immediately below it does no exception handling around `WT.queue`. `_leave_line` wraps `WT.clear` in `try/except (OSError, ValueError, TypeError)` with the comment "advisory", which shows these `waits` service calls are known to be able to raise on filesystem/state problems. Concrete failure: on a repo where the `waits.queue` write fails (read-only repo dir, ENOSPC, or a malformed/`TypeError`-producing argument), a claim that should be turned away with the reserved-for refusal instead propagates `OSError` out of `_refuse_if_reserved`/`_early_refusal`, so the caller gets an exception rather than the `Outcome` it was promised, and `_leave_line`/other callers never see the refusal. Wrapping the `WT.queue(...)` call the same way `_leave_line` wraps `WT.clear` would make the documented invariant hold.
chunk_findings.location: ddflow/api/lifecycle.py `_join_line` (new helper, ~line 1145 in the post-diff file)
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle.py `_join_line` (new helper, ~line 1145 in the post-diff file)

chunk_findings.detail: `_queue_path` maps `f"{agent}-q-{item}"` through a per-character filter that keeps only alphanumerics and `-_.` and replaces **every other character with `"_"`**. `"_"` is itself in the keep-set, so distinct `(agent, item)` pairs that differ only in an "unsafe" vs. an underscore character produce the same filename. For example `_queue_path(repo, "a/b", "task")` and `_queue_path(repo, "a_b", "task")` both yield `<dir>/a_b-q-task.json`; likewise agent `"a:b"`/`"a_b"`, or item `"x y"`/`"x_y"`. Since the path is the sole identity of a reserved place, two such agents now share one registration file. Their `queue()` read-modify-write clobbers each other's `since`/`until` (so a younger agent can inherit an older agent's `since`, or an agent can silently re-join when it should have lost its place), and `drop_queue()`/`take_place()` for one agent `unlink()`s the file that holds the other's reservation. The intended invariant ("older live waiter keeps its place", "a younger or unqueued claimant is refused with reserved-for") is violated for those inputs, because ordering is decided purely by the shared file's `since`. Note the adjacent `take_place` docstring explicitly relies on this path to hand a refusal's place to the following `wait`, so a collision also lets one agent's `wait` consume another agent's freshly-created place.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/waits.py:_queue_path

chunk_findings.detail: The predicate dereferences `w.woken` unconditionally, so any reservation record that predates the `woken` field (e.g. a waiter file/state entry written by the previous release, which the stated intent says must still "keep a freed file for a bounded window") is not handled gracefully. On an upgrade with existing reservation state, the predicate either raises `AttributeError` (if the record object has no `woken` attribute, which is the normal failure mode for attribute-style access on a record reconstructed without that member) or, if the deserializer supplies a `None` default, returns `False` because `isinstance(None, bool)` is false. In the first case the wait/claim path crashes instead of classifying the record; in the second the older-but-still-live reservation is silently treated as not live and stops blocking a younger or unqueued claimant, which is exactly the "older live waiter keeps a freed file" guarantee the change is supposed to provide. A defaulted check (`getattr(w, "woken", False)`) or a migration that backfills `woken=False` would be required to make pre-existing records behave as reserved.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/waits.py:261 (live-waiter predicate, `isinstance(w.woken, bool)`)

chunk_findings.detail: The test is named and intended to cover the headline case where the waiting process is *gone* ("Registration survives the wake as a deadline-only reservation"), but it never makes that process go away. `_wait_until_woken` runs `A.wait(...)` in a thread of the test process itself, so `WT.register` records the **test process's own, still-alive pid**. After `t.join(20)` the thread has ended but the pid is alive. Consequently the assertion `[(w.agent, w.item, w.woken) ...] == [(B, "TB", True)]` only verifies that a *woken waiter whose pid is still alive* keeps its place. The case that the feature actually guarantees — a woken registration surviving after the waiting pid has died — is never exercised. Concretely, a regression in which a woken reservation is dropped whenever its pid is dead (a natural mistake, since the code must *also* drop dead non-woken waiters, as `test_a_dead_waiter_never_blocks` requires) would make the reservation vanish immediately in production yet still pass this test, because the pid here never dies. The dead case is only covered for a *non-woken* waiter (`test_a_dead_waiter_never_blocks`), which asserts the opposite behavior (it must not block).
chunk_findings.title: test_a_woken_wait_keeps_its_place_after_its_process_is_gone

titles: ddflow/api/lifecycle.py `_join_line` (new helper, ~line 1145 in the post-diff file)

chunk_findings.detail:
`_hold_reserved` makes `next` offer *promoted* capped items: when a ready item is reserved for another live waiter, a slot is freed and the next item held back by the parallelism cap is moved into `p.ready` (`promoted = {i.id for i in kept if i.id in p.capped}`; `p.ready[:] = kept`). `_judge_any`, whose docstring is literally "the same ready set `next` offers", only iterates `p.ready` from `plan` and never looks at `p.capped`, so it can report nothing while `next` reports work.

Concrete case: `cfg.lease.waiter_reservation_s > 0`, parallelism cap = 1. Item `A` is the ready item and is covered by a live, older other-agent waiter's reservation; item `B` is free but was held back by the cap (it is in `p.capped`). `next` runs `_hold_reserved`: `A` is reserved, so it is appended to `p.blocked` and dropped, then `B` is promoted and `p.ready` becomes `[B]`; `next` returns `O.ok` with `ready == [B]`. A `wait` with no item routes to `_judge_any`, whose `p.ready == [A]`; `_claim_blocker(A, ..., repo=repo)` returns the reservation blocker, so `ready == []` and `wait` reports `status != ready` / nothing actionable. The two commands now contradict each other for the same state, and `wait` steers an agent away from an item `next`/`claim` would actually grant. Either `_judge_any` must run the same reservation/promotion pass over `p.ready + p.capped`, or the docstring/contract must change.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle.py `_judge_any` (line ~326) vs `next`/`_hold_reserved`

chunk_findings.detail:
`_reserved_for` decides whether a waiter `w` is allowed to keep a reservation by asking “would `w`’s own claim succeed?” via `_claim_blocker(st, cfg, target, w.agent, live, now, fair=False)`. Because `fair=False` suppresses the reservation check this whole feature adds, a waiter that is itself blocked by another waiter’s reservation is still treated as able to claim, which contradicts the function’s own contract (“A waiter reserves only while its own claim would succeed (it is not still behind someone else …)”).

Concrete scenario: waiter `C` holds a reservation for item `Z`; waiter `A` (older than claimant `B`) waits for item `X`, whose globs overlap `Z`’s, so `A`’s claim of `X` is refused with `reserved-for C`; claimant `B` is not queued for `Y`, and `Y`’s globs overlap `X`’s but not `Z`’s, and all three share a line key. Iterating `live_waiters` oldest-first, `_reserved_for` skips `C` (no conflict with `Y`), reaches `A`, passes the `conflicts(globs, list(target.globs), shared)` and `CF.line_key` tests, then calls `_claim_blocker(st, cfg, X, A, live, now, fair=False)`, which ignores `C`’s reservation and returns `None`, so `A` is returned and `B` is refused `… is reserved for A …` even though `A` cannot actually claim `X` at that moment. `B` (which would otherwise be free to take `Y`) is needlessly held for the whole reservation window. Passing `fair=True` here would recurse endlessly, so the bug is the flat recursion guard: the “would succeed” check needs to stay reservation-aware (e.g. via a depth/visited guard) while ignoring only `w` itself.
chunk_findings.title: `ddflow/api/lifecycle.py` → `_reserved_for` (the `_claim_blocker(..., fair=False)` call)

chunk_findings.detail: `live()` returns `True` unconditionally for a woken registration, but its only bound is the `until` deadline, and `until` defaults to `0.0`. The guard `if self.until and now > self.until: return False` is skipped whenever `until` is falsy, so `Waiter(until=0.0, woken=True).live(now)` returns `True` for every `now` (e.g. `now=1e18`), forever. A woken reservation has no process to fall back on, so `until` is the only thing that can lapse it; constructing/reading back any woken registration that never got a positive `until` (the dataclass default, and the value a no-timeout `wait` carries) produces an eternal reservation: the file is held and every younger/unqueued claimant is refused with `reserved for <agent>` indefinitely, contradicting both the config doc ("The place lapses this many seconds after the waiter could claim…") and the field comment ("…but only for a bounded time"). The type's own `live()` should reject/expire `woken` with a non-positive `until` rather than treating `until == 0` as "no deadline, so live" once the process is gone.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/waits.py:82 (Waiter.live)

chunk_findings.detail: queue() recovers `since` only from the queue-path file. After a wait wakes, the place is held in the wait's own registration updated by mark_woken, and take_place has already unlinked the queue file. If a claim is refused while that woken reservation is still live, queue() starts a new place with `since = now` rather than inheriting the reservation's earlier since. With window_s=10: A is refused at t=0 (queue file since=0), waits at t=1 (take_place drops the queue file, wait W since=0), wakes at t=2 (W.until=12), is refused again at t=3, so queue writes a place Q' with since=3 and until=13. At t=12.5 W has lapsed but Q' is still live, so A's effective since is 3; an agent C whose first refusal was at t=2 now outranks A even though A never stopped asking. This contradicts "Its place is its FIRST refusal; each refusal renews the deadline".
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/waits.py:queue

chunk_findings.detail: `_write(w)` is outside the try/except OSError. If the registry directory exists but is not writable, path.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True) and the .gitignore check succeed, then _write raises PermissionError, which propagates and can fail the claim, contradicting the docstring "an unwritable registry means no queue, never a failed claim." The same happens with ENAMETOOLONG for a prefix whose 80 truncated characters encode to more than 255 bytes.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/waits.py:queue

chunk_findings.detail: The comment states the reverse direction is being tested — "a waiter for TD does not hold up TC's claim of mcp.py once B has it" — but the code executes `_claim(proj, "TB", B)` at the end, and this assertion cannot observe anything about agent-d's reservation. By that point `agent-d` is a waiter for `TD` while C still holds `TD` (claimed by `_claim(proj, "TD", C).ok` earlier and never released), so `agent-d` is exactly the case the suite itself defines in `test_a_waiter_still_behind_another_holder_reserves_nothing`: a waiter behind another holder reserves nothing at all. Consequently the final `_claim(proj, "TB", B).ok` passes regardless of whether reservations are scoped to the waiter's own file (`src/other.py`) or wrongly cover `src/mcp.py`; the assertion would also pass if a `TD` waiter's reservation covered `mcp.py`, which is the exact bug the test purports to guard. A concrete input demonstrating the gap: if the implementation computed the reservation from a waiter's blocker set (the helper hardcodes `waiting_on=["HOT"]`) instead of the waiter's own `item`, `agent-d`'s reservation would land on `src/mcp.py`, yet this test still passes because `agent-d` is non-claimable (`TD` held by C). To exercise the intended direction the waiter's target must be free when the competing claim of `mcp.py` is made, or a different (non-waiter) claimant of `mcp.py` must be used.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_claim_fairness.py:test_waiters_on_disjoint_files_never_block_each_other

chunk_findings.detail: The new assertion assumes that this claim consumes the woken waiter's deadline-only reservation, but the claim is made with `no_worktree=True`. The intent describes the reservation as keeping a freed *file* (a worktree) for a bounded window; a no-worktree claim never takes that file, so the claim path does not exercise the worktree reservation and cannot spend it. Given the project state immediately after the release, `WT.live_waiters(proj)` therefore still contains the reservation, and the following assertion `WT.live_waiters(proj) == []` fails. To actually test that the reservation is spent, the claim must be made through the worktree-claiming path (i.e. without `no_worktree=True`, or with it explicitly false) so that the freed file is consumed.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_wait.py:68 (`A.claim(proj, "T2", no_worktree=True, agent=WAITER)`)

chunk_findings.detail: `_judge_any`'s docstring promises "the same ready set `next` offers", but the body only inspects `p.ready` (`refused = [(i, _claim_blocker(...)) for i in p.ready]`). After this change, `next` no longer offers `p.ready`: `_hold_reserved` drops reserved items and promotes items out of `p.capped` into `p.ready`, so `next` can offer an item that `_judge_any` never looks at, because it never reads `p.capped`. Before this change both paths used `p.ready` alone, so they agreed; now they do not. Concretely: with one free slot (`max_parallel = 1`, no live leases) and two eligible items `A`, `B`, `plan` produces `p.ready = [A]`, `p.capped = [B]` (the docstring of `_hold_reserved` confirms `plan` trims `ready` to the free slots and puts the rest in `capped`). If `A` is reserved for an older waiter, `next` drops `A` and promotes `B`, returning `O.ok` with `ready = [B]`. The `wait`-anything path calls `_judge_any`, whose `refused` list contains only `A` (refused with reserved-for), so `ready` is empty and the caller is told to block/wait even though the same codebase's `next` reports `B` as actionable. That is exactly the input where the two answers diverge, and it makes the "would waiting never end / can I start now" answer wrong.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle.py:326 (`_judge_any`)

chunk_findings.detail: `_end_wait` calls `WT.mark_woken(w, cfg.lease.waiter_reservation_s)`, passing a duration in seconds where the reservation logic expects an absolute deadline. The docstring describes the surviving registration as a “deadline-only reservation”, and the stored field is identified as `_reserved_for`, both of which imply `mark_woken` takes a deadline (e.g. `time.time() + cfg.lease.waiter_reservation_s`). With the current call and a typical positive value such as `waiter_reservation_s = 300`, the deadline is set to roughly epoch+300s — far in the past. `_early_refusal` then treats the reservation as already lapsed and allows a younger/unqueued claimant to acquire the freed item immediately. Reproduce: waiter A waits on item X, the holder releases X, A wakes and runs `_end_wait(..., keep=True, ...)`, then agent B calls `claim` for X; B is not refused with `reserved-for` and can acquire X. This defeats the core reservation behaviour.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle.py:_end_wait (the `WT.mark_woken` call)

chunk_findings.detail: `hashlib.sha1(f"{agent}\0{item}".encode(), usedforsecurity=False)` encodes the pair with strict UTF-8. On POSIX, `item` can be a file name containing bytes that are not valid UTF-8; Python represents such bytes as lone surrogates (e.g. a name with byte `0xff` is `"\udcff"`). `"x\udcff".encode()` raises `UnicodeEncodeError`. `queue()` calls `_queue_path()` before its `try/except`, so a refused claim for such an item raises instead of silently skipping the queue, directly violating the docstring’s “never a failed claim” advisory promise. `drop_queue()`/`take_place()` hit the same encoding failure. `os.fsencode` or `.encode("utf-8", "surrogateescape")` is required here.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/waits.py:_queue_path

chunk_findings.detail: `take_place()` unlinks the refused-claim place (`drop_queue`) before the wait registration is durable. Concrete interleaving: agent A holds queue file QA with `since=1000`; A calls `wait`, `take_place` reads `QA.since`, unlinks QA, and returns `1000`; before A’s caller writes its wait record, agent B (unqueued, `since=1010`) claims the item. Because there is now no record of A on disk, the reservation scan sees no older waiter and B’s claim is allowed, taking the item. A then starts waiting despite having held the oldest place. This is the very type of gap the reservation mechanism is meant to close, and the `drop_queue` docstring (“a `wait` for the item has taken it over”) is not true at the point it is called. QA should remain until the wait record is written, or the handoff should be an atomic rename.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/waits.py:take_place

chunk_findings.detail: `carried` is falsy exactly when the waiter has no older place — that is what the very next line, `keep = carried > 0`, asserts. So a waiter that starts a *fresh* wait on item X registers a record with `since = 0` (epoch 1970), not the time the place was made. When that waiter wakes ready for X, `_end_wait` turns this same record into the reservation that `_reserved_for` consults, and the only reason a place's `since` is carried at all is that "younger"/"older" is decided from these place times. A reservation stamped `since = 0` therefore ranks as older than every genuine place, so `_reserved_for` will refuse *any* queued claimant, including one that queued before this waiter — the opposite of the stated rule ("refuse a younger or unqueued claimant with reserved-for"). Repro: agent A queues for X at t=100 (claim refused, `_join_line`); agent B, never queued, calls `wait(X)` at t=200, so B's record gets `since=0`; X frees, B wakes and keeps a reservation whose `since=0`; A's claim for X is then refused with `reserved-for` although A's place is older than B's. The record's `since` should be stamped with the current time when `carried` is falsy, with `carried > 0` used only for the keep decision.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle.py:701 (`since=carried` in the wait registration)

chunk_findings.detail: `_refuse_if_reserved` bails out with `None` (i.e. "free, claim may proceed") whenever `st.items.get(item)` is `None`, before it ever consults `want`. But the whole point of the reservation is to keep a *freed file* for an older waiter, and a file can be claimed by an item name that is not (yet) in `st.items`. Concretely: a waiter W wakes off item A's file `f` and gets a deadline-only reservation on `f`; a new step B (not in `st.items`) is then claimed with `want=[f]` (the common first-claim / `next` case). `_refuse_if_reserved` sees `it is None`, returns `None`, and B's claim acquires the lease on `f`, so W's bounded reservation is silently bypassed — contrary to "older live waiter keeps a freed file" and "claim, wait and next refuse a younger or unqueued claimant with reserved-for". Note the sibling helper `_blocking_items` explicitly handles `it is None` (returning `[item]`), confirming absent-from-state items are expected on this path, and `_reserved_for` already receives the globs separately, so the refusal could be evaluated from `want` alone. The guard should only skip when there is neither an item nor any requested globs, not merely when the item is absent.
chunk_findings.location: ddflow/api/lifecycle.py:_refuse_if_reserved (the `if skip or it is None: return None` guard)
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle.py:_refuse_if_reserved (the `if skip or it is None: return None` guard)

chunk_findings.detail: The test's whole premise is that `waits.chmod(0o500)` makes `.ddflow/local/waits` unwritable, so the refused claim's attempt to register a place raises `EACCES`, and the assertion verifies the claim still returns `REFUSED` instead of propagating that error. Directory mode bits are not enforced for uid 0 (`CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE`), so in the common case where the suite runs as root (most Docker-based CI images are root by default), the registration write at `waits/…json` simply succeeds. The test then passes for the ordinary reason — the claim is refused by A's still-live `HOT` lease — and never exercises the unwritable-registry path at all. Demonstrated input: `pytest tests/test_claim_fairness.py::test_an_unwritable_registry_never_fails_the_refusal` executed as uid 0; `_claim(proj, "TC", C)` writes C's queue entry successfully, `out.exit == O.REFUSED` holds, and a regression that lets the `OSError` escape (or that loses the refusal) would still be green in exactly the environment the test was written to protect.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_claim_fairness.py::test_an_unwritable_registry_never_fails_the_refusal

titles: ddflow/api/lifecycle.py:_refuse_if_reserved (the `if skip or it is None: return None` guard)

chunk_findings.detail:
`_reserved_for` deliberately treats a bad registry as "no queue" by wrapping `WT.live_waiters(repo, now)` in `try/except (OSError, ValueError, TypeError)`, but the waiter objects it returns are then consumed unchecked. In particular `_reserved_msg` → `_fmt_since(w.since)` calls `datetime.fromtimestamp(t, tz=UTC)` outside any guard. A registry entry whose `since` is non-finite survives `live_waiters` (the comparisons `inf + x < now`, `now - inf` never raise and never mark it lapsed, so it is returned as live), and then `_fmt_since(float('inf'))` raises `OverflowError` (and `float('nan')` raises `ValueError`) — neither is caught. This value is trivially reachable: Python's `json.loads` accepts `Infinity`/`NaN` by default, so a registry file containing e.g. `"since": Infinity` parses and reads "successfully", defeating the stated advisory-fallback.

Reproduction: registry holds a single waiter for item `X` (globs `["f"]`) with `since = Infinity`, all files free; a fresh agent (no place, so `mine is None`) claims a conflicting item. `_reserved_for` iterates, `_claim_blocker(target, w.agent)` returns `None` (nothing older reserves), so it returns `w`; `_claim_blocker` then builds `Blocked(it.id, "conflict", _reserved_msg(...))`, and `_fmt_since(inf)` raises `OverflowError`, which propagates out of `_claim_blocker` and crashes `claim`/`wait`/`next` instead of degrading to "no reservation". Coercing/validating `w.since` (or formatting inside the existing `try`) would close the gap.

chunk_findings.detail: The registration comment promises two independent ways for a place to survive: "Woken for an item, **or** carrying an older place: the place in line stays on at the end." The code implements the first but overwrites the second. `keep` is initialised to `carried > 0`, but inside the wake branch it is unconditionally reassigned to `v["status"] == "ready" and bool(item)`. The explicit `== "ready"` test only makes sense because `_judge_wait` can return non-`"blocked"` statuses other than `"ready"` (otherwise the equality check would be dead code and `keep = bool(item)` would suffice). For any such status (e.g. the waited-for item disappears/changes so the judge reports it as no longer something to wait on, or a re-judge after an earlier wake no longer returns `"ready"`), a waiter that registered with `carried > 0` has `keep` reset to `False`, so the `finally` in `_end_wait` takes the `WT.unregister(w)` path instead of `WT.mark_woken(w, ...)`. The waiter that was holding an older place loses its reservation, contradicting the stated invariant and the `_end_wait` docstring ("A wait that WOKE for an item keeps its place in line"). The intended expression is `keep = keep or (v["status"] == "ready" and bool(item))`, so the carried place is retained unless the timeout path also had nothing to preserve.

chunk_findings.detail: The test writes `waiter_reservation_s = 1` and then requires the first post-wait `_claim(proj, "TC", C)` to observe the reservation. The reservation deadline is set by the child process when it wakes from `A.wait`; the parent only calls `_claim` after `p.wait(30)` returns, i.e. after the child's interpreter shutdown and the parent's scheduling latency. On a loaded runner this interval can exceed 1 s, so the first `_claim` succeeds instead of being refused and the assertion `refused == O.REFUSED` fails nondeterministically. The window must be widened, or the first claim must be synchronised directly to the wake.

chunk_findings.detail: `_dead_pid()` returns a pid that is immediately available for reuse. If the OS recycles that pid before `_claim(proj, "TC", C)` runs, `WT.live_waiters` sees the registration as live, the claim is refused as `reserved for B`, and `assert _claim(proj, "TC", C).ok` fails. The test is therefore flaky under pid churn; it needs a pid that is guaranteed not to be reusable (e.g. a sentinel or a non-existent pid chosen outside the allocatable range).
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_claim_fairness.py:test_a_dead_waiter_never_blocks

chunk_findings.detail: The reservation being tested is one where the older live waiter “keeps a freed file” (per the change intent), i.e. the reservation is scoped to the freed worktree/file. The test then spends that reservation by calling `A.claim(..., no_worktree=True)`, which claims a task without allocating or consuming a worktree. A no-worktree claim never touches the freed file, so it cannot consume a reservation that is held on that file. Concretely: after the waiter wakes with a reservation on the released file, the test issues a no-worktree claim for `"T2"`; the reservation on the released file remains live until its deadline, so the next assertion `WT.live_waiters(proj) == []` fails because the woken, deadline-only registration is still present. The test should claim a task in a way that actually uses the reserved file (e.g. drop `no_worktree=True`) to demonstrate that the claim spends the reservation.

chunk_findings.detail:
The `Waiter.path` field is documented (line ~78) as `path: str = ""  #: the registration file; not serialised`, and nothing in the new code sets `path` after a waiter is loaded back from the registry. So when `hold_place` finds its own previously-recorded waiter read from disk, `w.path` is `""`, while `str(path)` is the real queue-file path. The guard therefore evaluates `"" == "/…/…"` → `False` on every repeat refusal, `w.asks` is never incremented, and `asks` stays at the value written by the very first refusal (`1`). Since `reserves()` is `return self.asks != 1`, a polling agent's place can *never* leave the "pending" state no matter how many times it asks again.

Concrete demonstration: against a live lease, call the refused-claim path twice for the same `(repo, agent, item)`. The second call renews `until` but leaves `asks == 1`, so `reserves()` is `False`; `live_waiters` reports `asks == 1` (not `2`), and a competing agent's claim succeeds instead of being refused with `reserved for <agent>`. This directly contradicts the new docstring ("the second ask makes it real") and the added test `test_a_refused_claim_asked_again_keeps_its_place_without_typing_wait`, which asserts `[(w.agent, w.item, w.asks) …] == [(C, "TC", 2)]` and that B is refused with `f"reserved for {C}"` — both of which fail when `asks` remains `1`. The net effect is that refused claims are starved (they never reserve) rather than reserving on the repeat ask the change intends.

chunk_findings.detail: The diff adds a stateful `asks` counter and makes `reserves()` depend on it (`return self.asks != 1`), but only `note_refusal` ever writes `asks` (it sets `asks=1` on creation and does `w.asks += 1` on a repeat refusal). The `wait` code path records a real place in the *same* per-`(repo, agent, item)` registration file (that is what the shared `path`/`woken` design is for: a refusal is "a waiter that never typed `wait`"), and it does not reset `asks`. Concretely: agent C calls `claim(TC)` and is refused — a record is written with `woken=True, asks=1`, which correctly reserves nothing. C then actually types `wait` for `TC`; the wait path finds that existing record (it must, to preserve `since`/fairness ordering) and updates `until`/`woken` in place, leaving `asks==1`. Now `reserves()` returns False, so C holds no place — `next_` still offers `TC` and other agents are not blocked — and because `note_refusal` early-returns on any matching record with `woken=False` (it only renews/increments `if w.woken:`), subsequent refused claims can never lift `asks` above 1 either. The result is that an agent that explicitly typed `wait` (the strongest form of asking) is permanently treated as a non-reserving pending place for that item, which is worse than the pre-change behavior and contradicts the intent that the second ask "makes it real". The fix is for the `wait` path (or `reserves`/`note_refusal`) to reset `asks` to 0 when a real blocking place is recorded.
